content: For all existing recommendations and good practice statements, the title and web link for the corresponding WHO guidance are provided in the remarks section to facilitate easy access to additional information from the original source. Chapter 2 outlines the methodology and process for developing the consolidated guideline on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) of women living with HIV. This guideline includes 52 recommendations (six of which are new) and 22 good practice statements (five of which are new), all relevant to the SRHR of women living with HIV. These are organized into subsections based on topic areas and types of services. Chapter 5 discusses key issues related to the implementation of the recommendations, aiming to maximize their benefits. These discussions are based on input from the Guideline Development Group (GDG). Chapter 6 identifies research gaps and priorities as determined by the GDG. It also discusses elements of an inclusive approach to expanding the evidence base on SRHR for women living with HIV. Chapter 7 describes plans for disseminating, applying, monitoring, evaluating, and updating the guideline and its recommendations. Evidence supporting the six new recommendations was derived from four systematic reviews and summarized in GRADE tables. These tables provide the evidence base on effectiveness and are included in the guideline. Additionally, the systematic review search strategies and flow charts are available in a separate web supplement. The framework of the guideline emphasizes the values and preferences of women living with HIV, as expressed in the Global Values and Preferences Survey (GVPS). It advocates for a comprehensive, woman-centered approach to SRHR, grounded in gender equality and human rights principles. This foundation is represented in the framework by a pink circle, which is surrounded by an enabling environment (outer purple circle) and health interventions (central teal segments). These elements are detailed in Chapters 3 and 4, respectively, and are accompanied by relevant WHO recommendations and good practice statements, listed in Tables 1 and 2 of the Executive Summary. The guideline highlights the importance of addressing barriers such as social exclusion, marginalization, criminalization, gender-based violence, stigma, and gender inequality. These barriers must be considered when developing strategies to improve the accessibility, acceptability, uptake, equitable coverage, quality, effectiveness, and efficiency of services for women living with HIV. If left unaddressed, these barriers undermine the SRHR of women living with HIV. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), launched in 2016, emphasize the importance of leaving no one behind and prioritizing those furthest behind. Women living with HIV often face intersecting forms of discrimination and are denied basic human rights, particularly in healthcare. To achieve the SDGs by 2030, the health sector must eliminate barriers to SRH services for women living with HIV. An enabling environment for SRHR includes the following characteristics: Health workers must adopt inclusive, non-stigmatizing attitudes and behaviors that promote safety and equality. Healthcare providers and facility managers should be held accountable for failing to meet professional ethical standards and human rights principles. Care and treatment services should be delivered in a people-centered, non-judgmental manner, empowering women living with HIV to make informed decisions about their care. Necessary medical products and technologies must be available to support health workers in delivering services and creating an enabling environment. Health management information should be timely, reliable, and comprehensive, capturing determinants of good SRH for women living with HIV. This information should be accessible to health workers, women living with HIV, and the community to address clinical and non-clinical aspects of SRHR. Information gaps should be identified and addressed through appropriate research, including community-driven research. Health interventions must be accessible, acceptable, and of high quality, available at the time and place they are needed. Budgetary allocations and financing strategies play a critical role in creating an enabling environment for good health outcomes, universal health coverage, and cost-effective service delivery. Policies, regulations, and operational incentives must support an enabling environment for SRHR for all women living with HIV, including those who are healthcare workers themselves. Creating a supportive environment requires leadership and coalition-building across sectors, including meaningful engagement with the community of women living with HIV. The health system should lead these efforts to ensure a comprehensive approach. The WHO Health System Framework identifies key building blocks for creating an enabling environment for SRHR, including service delivery, health workforce, information, medical products and technologies, financing, and leadership/governance. These elements contribute to improved health outcomes, equity, responsiveness, and efficiency. Strategies for creating an enabling environment include: 1. Supporting women’s psychosocial health to reduce internalized stigma at the individual level. 2. Continuing HIV education in communities and supporting social protections to reduce stigma in social settings. 3. Ensuring healthcare facilities do not allow discriminatory practices to reduce institutional stigma. 4. Promoting policies and enacting laws that prevent stigma and discrimination to address stigma at its roots. Investing in long-term programming is essential. Examples include creating SRH and HIV program plans with a 10–15 year horizon, investing in capacity-building, and working to change destructive social norms. Long-term planning strategies and indicators can support sustainable goals, even if plans are implemented in five-year phases. Focusing on positive messages is critical. Interventions should identify and build on existing strengths among women living with HIV and within the health system. Techniques like appreciative inquiry can highlight achievements that serve as a foundation for future progress. An exclusive focus on negative experiences may retraumatize women without supporting recovery, healing, and resilience. The importance of language must be acknowledged. Positive, inclusive language creates opportunities for advancement and collaboration. For example, discussing “promoting health” instead of “ending disease” fosters a forward-looking perspective. Language should prioritize people over disease, such as using “people living with HIV” instead of “HIV-infected people.” Terms like “acquire” are more neutral than “infected” when referring to HIV transmission. Using “comprehensive prevention of vertical transmission” instead of “mother-to-child transmission” reduces potential blame on women living with HIV. Language plays a central role in creating an environment that promotes SRHR. Developing interventions in partnership with end-user communities ensures that services respond to the needs, priorities, and realities of intended beneficiaries. This approach supports the creation and maintenance of an enabling environment for SRHR for women living with HIV.
